record.file_problem: Repository metadata, README, and file list only; the code and listed result files were not read or run.
record.tranche_reason: The README reports refusal outcomes after direction-based abliteration, but uses a different intervention from the original: expert-selective or residual o_proj weight edits rather than projecting a single activation direction out at every layer and position.
record.gate_note: The README reports refusal rates after weight edits and expert masking, and capability checks after residual o_proj edits. KL values are described as confirming weight changes, not as refusal or capability outcomes; the prefill/decode Jaccard result is a routing comparison, not a measure named by a claim version. Neither is recorded as a row.
record.test_reason: The repo turns the refusal direction into weight edits on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, a released MoE instruct model. It edits selected expert down_proj weights (runs 1–3) or o_proj in all 48 layers (runs 4–6) and reports refusal rates. That bears directly on V2, abliteration as a practical weight edit. The intervention differs from the original's full orthogonalization of every residual-writing matrix, so it is T2 (and a new MoE setting).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that per-expert MoE abliteration does not reduce refusal in Qwen3-30B-A3B. They read high-scoring experts as compliance pathways. They find o_proj abliteration across all layers lowers refusal to about 75% with no capability damage, but it hits a ceiling. They attribute the failure to attention writing refusal before MoE and to the router routing around edited experts.
record.recipe_differences: This is a tool repo with reported experiments, not a replication. It scores experts using refusal-direction projections and edits expert down_proj or attention o_proj weights; it does not report the original activation-level projection at every layer and position or direction addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported refusal outcome varies with intervention target and strength: MoE down_proj edits leave refusal near 90%, while residual o_proj edits lower it progressively as strength rises. The README also reports different expert routing in prefill and decode.

fits_no_version.finding: Masking experts scored as refusal-related (via jailbreak decomposition, or decode-phase scoring) leaves refusal at 94–95%. This is higher than the edited runs, and the authors read these experts as compliance pathways.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE models, experts most aligned with the refusal direction or with harmful routing may carry compliance rather than refusal; masking them does not reduce refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Prefill and decode top-expert sets barely overlap (Jaccard 0.10, zero overlap in top 15).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert routing relevant to refusal differs between prompt processing and generation in MoE models.

record.problems: Evidence is reported for one model only. The README gives no prompt counts, uncertainty estimates, or detailed capability metrics beyond a stable reasoning canary and 0% over-refusal. Its narrative says refusal rose to 95.0% and 94.1%, while the table's unmodified baseline is ~100%, leaving those comparisons unclear.
record.rows_left_out: No behavioral outcomes were omitted. KL values are excluded because the README presents them as weight-change diagnostics, not refusal or capability measures; the prefill/decode Jaccard result is routing similarity rather than a claim-version outcome.

untested.parts: No full ablation of the difference-in-means direction from every residual writer or from activations; no direction addition to induce refusal. Capability retention was checked only after partial edits.
Full orthogonalization of all residual-writing matrices (embeddings, attention, all experts) as in the original recipe was not run. Only one model.
Multi-direction SVD editing of experts was run (runs 2–3) but was not compared against single-direction editing on the same target. It says nothing on whether refusal is a cone or affine.

missing.what: Per-run detail (prompt counts, refusal judge, utility and reasoning scores) in the run reports, plus residual test results and the research findings document; none were read.

record.verdict_notes: GitHub tool repo, not peer reviewed. Only the README was available. Evidence covers one model, with no prompt counts or uncertainty. The edit never orthogonalizes all residual writers, so incomplete removal limits this recipe on MoE rather than refuting the single-direction account. V1 is therefore left untested rather than limited.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test activation projection at every layer and position, addition of the direction to induce harmless-request refusals, or broad general capability beyond the stated reasoning canary and over-refusal check.
Only one instruct checkpoint is reported; it does not establish results across released models generally.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
Multi-directional ablation is mentioned, but the README does not test whether refusal is better described by an affine set, cone, or dominant direction plus others.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No cross-language or cross-model transfer test.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or stages.

source_check.notes: The text holds only the README and a file list. Per-run reports are not in it, and the README gives neither the eval prompt count nor the refusal judge. The baseline is approximate (~100%). The header's 'code: n' looks wrong, since the study is an Apache-2.0 Rust code repo. Runs 7–8 mask experts at inference time rather than editing weights, and both raised refusal (95.0%, 94.1%).
